quiz.title: Chapter 4 Quiz: Secondary Sources
quiz.intro: Ten questions on matching a secondary source to the question you are holding, and on using one without mistaking it for the law.

items.q: A no-clue exploratory question should send you first to:
options: A legal encyclopedia such as Am. Jur. 2d or C.J.S.
items.why: Encyclopedias give breadth and vocabulary, not depth; use one to learn the language and framework, then move on (Legal Encyclopedias; Matching Source Type to Question Type).

items.q: A survey question (how have multiple jurisdictions handled this?) is best answered by:
options: An ALR annotation, a Restatement, a 50-state survey, or a CRS report
items.why: ALR annotations focus on a narrow issue with case citations from many jurisdictions, exactly what a survey question demands (American Law Reports; the mapping table).

items.q: Words & Phrases differs from an ordinary legal dictionary because it:
options: Collects judicial definitions of terms from published opinions
items.why: That makes it more powerful when the precise judicial meaning of a term matters to your argument (Legal Dictionaries and Words & Phrases).

options: Published by the American Law Institute; persuasive, not binding, though some adopted sections carry strong weight
items.why: Courts cite Restatements frequently, and a section a court has adopted may earn a cite in a brief (Restatements of the Law).

items.q: What does the chapter call the most valuable part of a secondary source for a researcher?
options: The footnotes, because they are the bridge to primary authority
items.why: Each primary authority a secondary source hands you is a candidate answer to a question on your map (Secondary Sources and the Research Cycle).

items.q: When should you stop reading a secondary source?
options: Never; read it cover to cover
The moment your current question is answered, logging the rest as later questions
items.why: Navigate by table of contents and index, stop when the question is answered, mine the footnotes (Secondary Sources and the Research Cycle).

items.q: Which evaluation questions does the chapter say to ask of any secondary source?
options: How long is it and who published it
Who wrote it, what their expertise is, the venue, when it was last updated, and the intended audience
Whether it cites your jurisdiction’s supreme court
items.why: Reliability determines how much weight the source deserves and how hard to verify it (How Secondary Sources Are Made).

items.q: In most court filings, secondary sources are:
options: Not cited as authority, with narrow exceptions like an adopted Restatement section or a leading treatise on an unsettled point
items.why: Know your context: what is out of place in a brief may be exactly what a law review article needs (Citing Secondary Sources in Legal Writing).

options: A nonpartisan Library of Congress report explaining a policy or legal issue, free online
items.why: Congressional Research Service reports are free at crsreports.congress.gov (Congressional Research Service Reports).

options: A secondary source can quietly fall out of date, so check the edition date and pocket part before trusting it
items.why: A major treatise published five years ago may be badly out of date in a fast-moving area (Common Pitfalls).
